# 0 Examinable Scope

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide gives its range as **Chapters 1–5, 7–11 and 13**, and lists the
examinable sections by number. For most of them it prints the section title only,
with no definitions, formulas or worked examples beneath it. Those sections are
collected here as a revision checklist so the scope is complete; the sections the
guide does develop have lessons of their own.

## Sections listed without content

| Chapter | Sections |
|---|---|
| **1 Quadratics** | 1.6 Solving quadratic equations · 1.7 Quadratic functions and their graph |
| **2 Polynomials** | 2.6 Solving polynomial equations by factoring |
| **3 Inequalities** | 3.2 Polynomial inequalities in one variable |
| **4 Functions** | 4.2 Operations on functions · 4.5 Inverse functions · 4.8 Partial fractions, rational functions · 4.9 The binomial theorem |
| **5 Exponentials and logarithms** | 5.3 Exponential functions · 5.6 Law of logarithms · 5.7 Exponential equations, changing bases |
| **8 Trigonometric graphs** | 8.4 Relationships among the functions · 8.5 Solving more difficult trigonometric equations |
| **9 Triangle trigonometry** | 9.2 The area of a triangle · 9.3 The law of sines · 9.4 The law of cosines · 9.5 Applications of trigonometry to navigation and surveying |
| **10 Trigonometric identities** | 10.1 Formulas for $\cos(A+B)$ and $\sin(A+B)$ · 10.2 Formulas for $\tan(A+B)$ · 10.3 Double-angle and half-angle formulas |
| **13 Sequences and series** | 13.1 Arithmetic and geometric sequences · 13.3 Arithmetic and geometric series and their sums · 13.4 Limits of infinite sequences · 13.5 Sums of infinite series · 13.6 Sigma notation · 13.7 Mathematical induction |

These are on the examination, and the section titles are the whole of what the
guide says about them. The formulas they name — the laws of sines and cosines, the
compound-angle and double-angle formulas, the binomial theorem, the sum formulas
for series — are not printed anywhere in the guide, so they are not reproduced
here either.

# 3.4 Linear Programming

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four parts of a linear program

**Linear programming** is a mathematical model consisting of a **linear function to
be optimised** — maximised or minimised — **and a set of inequalities representing
the restrictions on resources**.

| Part | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised. It might represent amounts of money earned or spent, goods manufactured or delivered, or any of a variety of other quantities |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |

The central fact, and the reason the method works at all: **if a linear program has
a solution, it will occur at a vertex — a corner point — of the feasible region.**
If there are multiple solutions, **at least one of them will occur at a vertex**.

That is what turns an infinite search into a finite one. The feasible region
contains infinitely many points, but only its corners need to be tested.

## Method

1. **Solve the system of linear inequalities.** Determine the coordinates of the
   vertices of the feasible region — that is, solve the system of equations
   consisting of the lines whose intersection is the vertex
2. **Evaluate the objective function** to be optimised at each vertex
3. **Identify the maximum or minimum value** of the objective function

## When two vertices tie

If **two vertices of the feasible region are both solutions** to a linear program,
then **every point on the line segment connecting the two vertices is also a
solution**.

This follows from the objective function being linear: if it takes the same value
at both ends of a segment, it takes that value all along it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Linear programming** | A model consisting of a linear function to be optimised and a set of inequalities representing restrictions on resources |
| **Objective function** | The function to be maximised or minimised in a linear program |
| **Constraints** | The linear inequalities of a linear program |
| **Feasible region** | The solution of the system of linear inequalities |
| **Vertex** | A corner point of the feasible region, where a solution will occur if one exists |

The guide treats this section as three pairings, each function set beside its
inverse:

- The **sine** function and the **inverse sine** function
- The **cosine** function and the **inverse cosine** function
- The **tangent** function and the **inverse tangent** function

That is the whole of what the guide prints for 7.5 — it names the three pairs and
develops none of them. No domains, ranges, graphs or principal values are given,
so none are supplied here.

The one place the guide does say something substantive about these functions is
**10.4**, where it notes that inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving
trigonometric equations and inequalities, but that **solutions may need to be
modified because of domain restrictions**. That restriction is the reason the

# 8.2 Sine and Cosine Curves

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The three measurements of a sinusoid

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles the graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between the function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | Determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values of the function |

Amplitude and midline are the two halves of the same calculation: the **half
difference** of the extremes gives the amplitude, and their **average** gives the
midline. Together they fix the vertical position and reach of the curve, which is
why 8.3 uses them as the route from a graph back to an equation.

## The four transformations

| Transformation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal dilation** | $y = \sin(bx)$ and $y = \cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | $y = a\sin x$ and $y = a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | $y = \sin(x + c)$ and $y = \cos(x + c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | $y = \sin x + d$ and $y = \cos x + d$ |

The guide also lists **reflecting a trigonometric function** as part of this
section, without giving its form.

Each constant acts on one measurement above: $b$ changes the frequency, $a$ the
amplitude, $d$ the midline, and $c$ shifts the curve horizontally without altering
any of the three.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Frequency** | The number of cycles a sinusoidal graph completes in an interval of $2\pi$ radians |
| **Amplitude** | Half the difference between a sinusoidal function's maximum and minimum values |
| **Midline** | The line determined by the average of the maximum and minimum values |
| **Horizontal dilation** | The transformation $y=\sin(bx)$ or $y=\cos(bx)$ |
| **Vertical dilation** | The transformation $y=a\sin x$ or $y=a\cos x$ |
| **Horizontal translation** | The transformation $y=\sin(x+c)$ or $y=\cos(x+c)$ |
| **Vertical translation** | The transformation $y=\sin x + d$ or $y=\cos x + d$ |

# 8.3 Modelling Periodic Behaviour

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Modelling runs in the opposite direction to 8.2: there, constants were given and
the curve followed; here the behaviour is observed and the constants must be
recovered from it.

## Recovering period and frequency

**The smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output
values start to repeat** can be used to determine or estimate the **period and
frequency** for a sinusoidal function model.

## Recovering amplitude and vertical shift

**The maximum and minimum output values** can be used to determine the
**amplitude and vertical shift** for a sinusoidal function model.

This is 8.2's amplitude and midline calculation used in reverse: the half
difference of the observed extremes gives the amplitude, and their average gives
the vertical shift.

## Choosing sine or cosine

**Flexibly select sine or cosine functions based on the situation**, making the
equation easier to calculate as well as promoting critical thinking.

The two curves differ only by a horizontal translation, so either can model the
same behaviour — but one will usually need a smaller phase shift than the other,
and that is the one worth choosing.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Period** | Determined from the smallest interval of input values over which the maximum or minimum output values start to repeat |
| **Vertical shift** | Determined, with the amplitude, from the maximum and minimum output values |

# 10.4 Solving Trigonometric Equations and Inequalities

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide carries the syllabus's own sub-codes here, which are given alongside each
statement below.

## Equations

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
equations.**

**Because trigonometric functions are periodic, there are often infinitely many
solutions to trigonometric equations** (10.4.A.3). This is the fact everything else
in the section responds to — every method below is a way of cutting an infinite
solution set down to the ones being asked for.

**Algebraic and graphical methods are used to solve trigonometric equations in a
finite interval, including the use of trigonometric identities and factorisation**
(10.4.A.4).

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving equations involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions.** An inverse returns one value where the equation has infinitely
many, so the others must be recovered by hand.

**In trigonometric equations arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.A.6).

## Inequalities

The same three points carry over.

**Equivalent trigonometric forms may be useful in solving trigonometric
inequalities.**

**Inverse trigonometric functions are useful in solving inequalities involving
trigonometric functions, but solutions may need to be modified due to domain
restrictions** (10.4.B.2).

**In trigonometric inequalities arising from a contextual scenario, there is often a
domain restriction that can be implied from the context, which limits the number of
solutions** (10.4.B.3).

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Equivalent trigonometric forms** | Rewritings of an expression that may make an equation or inequality solvable |
| **Domain restriction** | A limit on the input values, either from an inverse function or implied by the context, which reduces the number of solutions |

# 11.1 Polar Coordinates and Graphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The polar coordinate system

The **polar coordinate system** is an alternative to the Cartesian system of
rectangular coordinates for locating points in a plane.

The polar coordinates of a point $P$ consist of an **ordered pair** $(r,\theta)$:

- $r$ is the **directed distance from the pole** to $P$
- $\theta$ is the **measure of the angle from the polar axis to** $OP$

The polar coordinates of the pole $O$ are $(0,\theta)$ — the distance is zero
whatever the angle, so the pole has infinitely many representations.

The angle $\theta$ can be measured in **degrees or radians**, and **both $r$ and
$\theta$ can be either positive or negative**. That last point is what the two
rules below exist to settle.

## The sign of the angle

| Sign of $\theta$ | How the polar angle is obtained |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | Rotating $OP$ **counterclockwise** from the polar axis |
| **Negative** | Rotating $OP$ **clockwise** from the polar axis |

## The sign of the distance

| Sign of $r$ | Where the polar distance is measured |
|---|---|
| **Positive** | From $O$ **along the terminal side** of the angle $\theta$ |
| **Negative** | From $O$ **on the ray opposite** the terminal side of the angle $\theta$ |

A negative $r$ therefore places the point on the far side of the pole from where
the angle points — which is why the same point has more than one set of polar
coordinates.

## Naming the plane

A plane is called an **$r\theta$-plane** when polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ are
used to identify its points.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Polar coordinate system** | An alternative to the Cartesian system for locating points in a plane |
| **Polar coordinates** | The ordered pair $(r,\theta)$ giving a point's directed distance from the pole and the angle from the polar axis |
| **Pole** | The origin $O$ of the polar system, with coordinates $(0,\theta)$ |
| **Polar axis** | The reference ray from which the angle $\theta$ is measured |
| **Terminal side** | The side of the angle along which a positive polar distance is measured |
| **$r\theta$-plane** | A plane whose points are identified by polar coordinates |
